extracted.intended_audience: NLP and patent informatics researchers and practitioners developing/evaluating LLMs and datasets for patent tasks
extracted.subtask_description: Benchmarks, dataset design, evaluation metrics, and failure modes for applying and evaluating language models on patent-specific tasks such as claim generation, subject classification, summarization, retrieval, and language modeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent document components
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent documents typically include the following elements: title, bibliometric information, patent classification code, citations, abstract, drawings, detailed description, and claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although format and content may vary by jurisdiction, include these elements when preparing patent corpora or when using patents as input for models; these elements are integral components of the patenting process and publicly accessible once a patent is issued.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM challenges for patent tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Jiang and Goetz identified three key challenges for LLMs in patent-related tasks: handling the long context length, processing technical language, and satisfying precision requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design datasets, models, and evaluation to explicitly address long contexts, domain technical terminology, and strict precision constraints required by patent texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: International Patent Classification (IPC) hierarchical labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The IPC system classifies patents into hierarchical levels (section, class, subclass, group, subgroup). Example: F → F02 → F02D → F02D 41 → F02D 41/02.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use IPC labels (section/class/subclass) for subject classification tasks; IPC (or CPC) hierarchies facilitate multi-level classification and comparison with prior work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer claims for subject classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are more specific and legally representative of the invention and thus more discriminative for patent subject classification than abstracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When training classifiers, prefer claims as input rather than abstracts: models fine-tuned on claims outperformed abstract-based models by roughly 3–7% across section/class/subclass levels in reported experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset inclusion for preference pairs (application vs granted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct preference datasets using pairs of the application (initially rejected) and the granted version; the EPD dataset filters patents with both versions and description lengths under 8,000 tokens to obtain preference pairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filter candidate patents to ensure both versions exist and limit description length (e.g., < 8,000 tokens) to create reliable human-annotated or naturally occurring preference labels for RLHF or preference learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification evaluation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score to evaluate patent subject classification models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute these metrics with standard libraries (the paper uses sklearn); report multi-class metrics at each hierarchical level (section/class/subclass) to capture performance granularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text-generation evaluation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use BLEU, ROUGE (R-1, R-2, R-L), and BERTScore to evaluate claim generation and summarization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure summarization with ROUGE variants and claim generation with BLEU/ROUGE/BERTScore (the authors use the Huggingface evaluate library). Compare across prior benchmarks (e.g., HUPD) and new datasets to quantify domain/time/jurisdiction gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Token counting / language-modeling corpus metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Count tokens using a consistent tokenizer (the paper uses tiktoken with the GPT-4o tokenizer) to measure corpus size and to compute claim length statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the same tokenizer for dataset and model tokenization statistics so token-based cutoff lengths and statistics are comparable across experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim length (tokens per claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim length is computed as the total token count divided by the number of claims for a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use claim length as a basic quantitative feature and as an input to analyses (e.g., claim-length correlates with classification and generation behaviors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural complexity (subordinate clause ratio)
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural complexity is determined by the ratio of subordinate clauses to the total number of sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extract subordinate-clause counts (authors used spaCy) and report this ratio as a measure of grammatical/structural complexity of claims; higher ratios indicate more syntactically complex claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntactic tree depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Syntactic tree depth is computed using a constituency parser and measures the depth of the syntactic parse tree of the main independent claim; higher values indicate more deeply nested grammatical structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report syntactic tree depth to capture nesting/complexity that may affect model performance on generation and parsing tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability: Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level
rubrics_metrics.description: Readability is evaluated using the Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level formula; a lower score indicates greater readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute readability with a textstat library and use it to compare patents across time/jurisdictions or to analyze generation quality (easier-to-read claims may be preferable for some downstream uses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lexical diversity: MTLD
rubrics_metrics.description: Lexical diversity is calculated by MTLD (Measure of Textual Lexical Diversity); higher values indicate more varied vocabulary and less repetition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MTLD to assess vocabulary variety in claims or generated texts; lexical diversity may correlate with perceived quality or redundancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term density (technical terminology concentration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Term density is calculated as the proportion of proper nouns and named entities and reflects the concentration of technical terminology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report term density to quantify how technical or named-entity-heavy patent texts are; useful for domain adaptation and model input selection decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain automated evaluation scores using an LLM-as-a-judge prompt (the paper uses a specific prompt in Table 13) with inference settings temperature=0.1 and top_p=0.95.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use LLM evaluators consistently (prompt + temperature/top_p) when applying LLM-as-judge; be aware of prompt design impact and calibrate against human judgments where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting reward-model overfitting / suspiciously high reward accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewarding accuracy achieving exceptionally high scores (e.g., >98% during DPO) can indicate overfitting to superficial patterns rather than meaningful quality distinctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate high reward accuracy as a red flag: check whether the reward model is exploiting simple heuristics (e.g., claim length, presence of specific legal terms) and not capturing substantive technical/legal quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common claim-generation anti-patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed low-quality outputs include: an excessively long overloaded independent claim, redundancy in dependent claims, and frequent overuse of terms such as 'wherein' and 'configured to'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these anti-patterns as qualitative error categories when auditing generated claims; aim for concise independent claims, minimal redundancy in dependencies, and varied syntactic phrasing where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference-dataset construction guidance for RLHF
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct application of application→granted transformations as preferences does not necessarily yield an effective preference dataset for RLHF; datasets should be refined or include human-annotated preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To build better RLHF datasets, incorporate more human-annotated preferences, curate or reweight examples to avoid superficial correlates, and consider more sophisticated RLHF formulations beyond direct DPO on naive preference pairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate separately on difficulty strata
rubrics_metrics.description: Report model performance separately on 'difficult' and 'easy' samples to reveal differing effects of training/optimization techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stratified evaluation (e.g., Tables showing BLEU/ROUGE/BERTScore on difficult vs easy examples) to diagnose where methods help or hurt; methods like DPO may degrade performance on both strata or more on difficult examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt and inference settings for claim generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Example prompt: 'You are a patent expert. Given the following patent description, generate patent claims.' Inference settings used: max new tokens=1024, temperature=0.1, top_p=0.95.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document and standardize prompts and decoding settings when comparing claim-generation methods; small changes to prompt or decoding hyperparameters can materially affect generation quality and evaluation metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use IPC codes for label consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of overlap between IPC and CPC, the paper uses IPC codes as labels for consistency with prior work (e.g., Suzgun et al., 2024) when performing subject classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a consistent classification taxonomy (IPC or CPC) across datasets/experiments to enable comparisons with prior benchmarks and to avoid label mapping inconsistencies.
